scenes.title: Foundation: derivatives, limits and continuity
scenes.objective: Recall the ideas behind Taylor and L'Hôpital.

ask.q: What is the derivative of eˣ at every real x?
ask.nudge: The exponential function is its own derivative.

body: Taylor's theorem approximates a smooth function near a point using derivatives at that point. L'Hôpital's rule compares derivatives when a quotient has an indeterminate form.
Uniform continuity strengthens ordinary continuity by requiring one δ to work across the entire domain. These ideas connect local approximation, limit evaluation and global control of variation.

items.recall: A polynomial built from derivatives of f at a centre a: Σ f⁽ᵏ⁾(a)(x−a)ᵏ/k!.
refresh: The constant term is f(a), the linear term is f′(a)(x−a), and higher terms use higher derivatives at a. The degree-n polynomial matches the first n derivatives at the centre.
The polynomial is a local approximation. Taylor's theorem supplies a remainder term that measures the error; a formal series alone does not guarantee equality with the function.

items.ask: What are the two standard indeterminate forms for L'Hôpital's rule?
refresh: The rule applies to a quotient whose numerator and denominator both tend to zero, or both become unbounded, under the theorem's differentiability and denominator conditions.
It does not directly apply to forms such as 0·∞, ∞−∞ or 1^∞. Rewrite those expressions as a quotient or use logarithms before considering the rule.

items.recall: For every ε>0 there is a δ>0 that works for all x,y in the domain.
refresh: Ordinary continuity allows δ to depend on the point x. Uniform continuity requires one δ for the entire domain, so the function cannot change too rapidly in some remote region.

Every continuous function on a closed bounded interval is uniformly continuous. A continuous function on an open or unbounded domain need not be uniformly continuous; 1/x on (0,1) is a standard counterexample.

scenes.title: Local approximation versus global control
scenes.objective: Distinguish Taylor approximation from uniform continuity.

ask.q: Does a Taylor polynomial give the exact value of every smooth function?
ask.nudge: Only when the remainder is zero or when convergence is established.

body: A Taylor polynomial uses local derivative information to approximate a function near a centre. The remainder theorem tells us how large the error can be.
Uniform continuity is different: it controls changes over the whole domain with a single δ. A function can be continuous everywhere but fail this global condition near a boundary or at infinity.

scenes.title: Taylor's theorem and remainder
scenes.objective: State the polynomial and the Lagrange remainder.

ask.q: Write the degree-two Taylor polynomial of f at a.

blocks.body: If f has n+1 derivatives on the interval, f(x)=Tₙ(x)+Rₙ(x), where Rₙ(x)=f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)(x−a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)! for some ξ between a and x.
If |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(t)|≤M between a and x, then |Rₙ(x)|≤M|x−a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)!.

scenario.teaser: A numerical method needs a certified approximation error.
scenario.title: Taylor approximation in numerical computation
body: A numerical algorithm may replace eˣ or sin x with a low-degree polynomial near a chosen centre. The polynomial is cheap to evaluate, but its accuracy must be justified.
Taylor's theorem supplies a remainder term. If the next derivative is bounded by M, the error is at most M|x−a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)! for the degree-n approximation.
This gives a practical way to choose the polynomial degree for a required tolerance. The bound is a guarantee; simply observing that the next term is small is not always a proof.

blocks.body: A function may have derivatives of every order without equalling its Taylor series everywhere. Use a theorem or a known convergence result before replacing a function by an infinite series.

scenes.problem: Find the degree-two Maclaurin polynomial for cos x.
hints: Evaluate f(0), f′(0) and f′′(0) for f=cos x.
scenes.solution: For cos x, f(0)=1, f′(0)=0 and f′′(0)=−1. Thus T₂(x)=1−x²/2.

scenes.title: L'Hôpital's rule
scenes.objective: Apply the rule only to valid indeterminate quotients.

ask.nudge: The quotient is 0/0; differentiate numerator and denominator.

blocks.body: For a 0/0 or ∞/∞ quotient, under suitable differentiability conditions and with denominator derivative non-zero near the point, the limit equals lim f′(x)/g′(x), if that latter limit exists.

After differentiating numerator and denominator, check the new form. You may apply the rule again only if the resulting quotient is still an eligible indeterminate form and the conditions continue to hold.
0·∞, ∞−∞, 0⁰, 1^∞ and ∞⁰ are not direct quotient forms. Algebraic rewriting or logarithms may convert them into 0/0 or ∞/∞.

scenes.title: Guided: a logarithmic limit
scenes.objective: Use L'Hôpital to evaluate a standard limit.
hints: As x→0, numerator and denominator both tend to zero.
scenes.solution: The form is 0/0. L'Hôpital gives lim [1/(1+x)]/1=1.

ask.q: Can L'Hôpital be applied directly to 0·∞?
ask.nudge: No; rewrite the product as a quotient first.

scenes.title: Uniform continuity: one δ for the whole domain

ask.q: Why is x² uniformly continuous on [0,1] but not on all of R?
ask.nudge: On a compact interval the slope is bounded; on R it grows without bound.

body: Uniform continuity requires that for every ε there is a single δ such that |x−y|<δ implies |f(x)−f(y)|<ε for every pair in the domain.

A continuous function on a closed bounded interval is uniformly continuous. On an unbounded domain the same may fail: x² changes increasingly rapidly as x grows. The condition is global, not pointwise.

scenario.teaser: A single tolerance must work across an entire operating range.
scenario.title: Uniform continuity in numerical stability
body: A numerical procedure may perturb its input by at most δ and require the output to change by less than ε. If δ can be chosen independently of the input location, the function is uniformly continuous on the domain.

On a compact interval, continuity guarantees this property. On an unbounded domain, a function such as x² is continuous but not uniformly continuous because the same input perturbation can create larger output changes farther out.
This is why the domain matters. Always state the interval or set when deciding uniform continuity.

body: 2. Remainder: f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(ξ)(x−a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)!; bound the next derivative for an error estimate.
3. Maclaurin means a=0; use standard expansions carefully.
4. L'Hôpital is for eligible 0/0 or ∞/∞ quotients under its hypotheses.
